items.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2024 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Kind of what Einstein was looking for, a “unified field theory.”

ctx.x: Oh yeah. There’s a difference. Let’s see, now see this is complicated because one tune has got two chords, another tune has a million chords. So here again is the psychology stuff. There’s a certain — when you’re dealing with harmonic movement that’s only two

beats — so the harmony is moving at a quick pace. It’s not there for four bars, eight bars. But it’s moving every two bars. And the tempo is at a good clip. So there is a way that you have to look at all of that harmonic minutiae and there’s a way that you have to look at a broader arc over that, which means you really do have to have your ears on and think melodically at the same time that you’re adhering to time and space. So here again you’re really walking and chewing gum at the same time. And see here’s…

such thing, maybe there is. But I always try to look at what is the one thing that I can maybe — the form of mentation that might give me the best results. Is there one thing, of all of the many things and ways to think of things, what is the one thing that will amalgamate all these moving parts and all these brain departments and functionality. And then for me it’s rhythm. Rhythm. Phrasing. That’s for me. And my melodic ear is on. It’s on, I have it on. There are certain things that I would say is static.…
